claims.claim: A one-to-many relationship links two tables so that one row in the first table can match many rows in the second, while each row in the second table matches exactly one row in the first.
One-to-many is the most common type of relationship in relational databases; Microsoft Learn states this directly and gives the example of a single teacher teaching many classes.

The canonical one-to-many example is a customer with many orders: W3Schools shows a Persons table and an Orders table in which the PersonID column in the Orders table points to the PersonID column in the Persons table, so one person can have many orders while each order references one person.
A one-to-many relationship is implemented by placing a foreign key column on the many side; each row there stores the primary key value of the one row it belongs to.

The underlying mechanism is the foreign key constraint: a foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column must match the values appearing in some row of another table, which maintains referential integrity between two related tables.

The same one-to-many link can be read from either end: Microsoft Learn lists one-to-many and many-to-one as the two names for the same shape, so a customer has many orders (one-to-many) and each order belongs to one customer (many-to-one).

One-to-many differs from many-to-many: in a many-to-many relationship, a row on either side can match more than one row on the other side, as with students attending many classes and each class having many students.

Because everyday hierarchies (parent/child rows, product categories with many products, departments with many employees) all share the one-to-many shape, understanding this one pattern explains the design of most real databases.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which table is called A and which is B in the one-to-many definition, and whether the direction is named one-to-many or many-to-one.
positions: Microsoft Learn defines one-to-many as 'each row in table B can match more than one row in table A, but each row in table A can match only one row in table B', and also lists many-to-one as a separate relationship type with the same underlying shape.
W3Schools describes the structure through the Persons/Orders example without using the phrase one-to-many, naming the sides child table and parent table.
PostgreSQL documents the foreign key mechanism (orders referencing products) without labeling cardinality at all.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All three sources describe the same structure: one row on one side, many rows on the other, with the reference stored on the many side. The lesson fixes its own consistent lettering (the 'one' table is A, the 'many' table is B), names both directions (has many / belongs to; one-to-many / many-to-one) so any source's phrasing maps cleanly, and avoids presenting any single convention as the only correct one.
